title: All fun and games
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino argues against the common assumption that boxes of games, card sorts and information hunts are ideal for low-attaining classes. Drawing on her own regretful early-career lessons, including a Periodic Table murder mystery that left students remembering nothing a week later, she shows how game rules and logistics load working memory and waste transition time. She uses cognitive load and Teach Like a Champion's transaction-cost idea to frame the critique, and she admits that one information-hunt lesson badly distressed an anxious student. She is not against all games, and defends Quizlet Live because its rules are simple and the content stays the focus. Her test is what students were thinking about by the end of the activity.
points: Games that introduce new content impose rules-plus-content load that is heaviest on pupils with weak memory.
Card sorts and information hunts burn lesson minutes on handing out, collecting and moving, which are transaction costs that do not involve thinking about content.
A low-extraneous-load game with simple rules, such as Quizlet Live used for revision, can be defensible.
The test of any game is what students were thinking about, the content or the game itself.
quotes: The following week, not a single student remembered any details from the game. All they remembered was sitting with their friends and trying to solve a puzzle they had no way of understanding.
If using games to introduce a topic or concept, the cognitive load of such a task would be overwhelming for any child but even more so for those that struggle with their memory.

In TLAC (Teach Like A Champion- get the book already!), we read about reducing transaction costs and how every minute matters. If the students are not thinking about the content, they are not learning.

It was this lesson that jolted me and resulted in me not using an information hunt since. I didn’t know it at the time, but a student in the class was in the process of getting a diagnosis of Autism and anxiety.
The reason I like using Quizlet Live sometimes is because there are no complicated rules. All the students have to do is answer the questions collaboratively.

At the end of the game, what have your students been thinking about? If it was the game itself or the fun they had answering the questions, it was a waste of lesson time no matter how engaged they were.
